claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in single-phase high-entropy alloys enhances local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation nucleation and glide.
Atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice distortion governs hardness and strength in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Lattice-distortion strengthening dominates over grain-boundary contributions when phase stability and grain size are maintained.
Arc melting followed by homogenization can produce a uniform, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi solid solution without secondary phases.
Replacing 5–10 at.% Ni with a larger atom such as Cu or Zr increases overall atomic size mismatch.
The proposed Ni substitution can retain a single-phase structure.
Atomic-size-mismatch-induced heterogeneous strain fields serve as primary barriers to dislocation glide when secondary phases are absent.
Enhanced atomic size mismatch increases the density of local strain fields that act as dislocation pinning sites.
The local strain fields increase the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation.
The local strain fields reduce dislocation mobility.
Increasing atomic size mismatch will increase hardness and yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The compositionally modified alloy will exhibit greater lattice strain in X-ray diffraction measurements than the baseline alloy.
In situ TEM under load will show fewer mobile dislocations in the modified alloy than in the baseline alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature to single-phase high-entropy alloys with comparable grain sizes and secondary-phase contents.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when phase transformations, diffusion, or grain-boundary sliding dominate.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes alloys in which the compositional change causes phase transformation, but the falsification rule treats observed secondary-phase formation as grounds for rejecting the hypothesis. Such an observation would place the experiment outside the stated domain rather than decisively falsify the in-domain mechanism.

The intervention permits either Cu or Zr substitution over a loosely specified amount, while the conditions state that the only variation is a controlled composition change aimed at lattice distortion. Changing elemental identity also changes chemical interactions and potentially phase stability, so the comparison does not isolate atomic size mismatch as the only varying material factor.
